title: 1x1 ribbed scarf
subtitle: A reversible, stretchy scarf that wraps close to the neck.
excerpt: A straight scarf worked flat in 1x1 rib on 4.5 mm needles with DK yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide and 175 cm long. The alternating knit and purl columns make a fabric that is fully reversible and stretches comfortably around the neck.
sourceNotes: 1x1 ribbing (alternating knit and purl stitches) is one of the oldest edging and fabric structures in knitting. Weldon's Practical Knitter describes it extensively for collars, cuffs, and neckwear. Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitting stitch pattern formed by alternating one knit stitch and one purl stitch across every row, with the knit stitches stacked above knit stitches and purl stitches above purl stitches. Produces a stretchy, reversible fabric with vertical columns.
A cast-on method that forms a neat, elastic edge using the tail and working yarn together. Produces one row of knitting as it sets up.

A cast-off method that produces an edge with more give than the standard cast off. Knit two stitches, pass the first over the second as usual, but return the remaining stitch to the left needle, knit it together with the next stitch, and repeat. Sometimes called the decrease cast-off.

content.text: This is a flat scarf worked from one short end to the other in 1x1 rib on 4.5 mm needles with DK yarn. It finishes at 18 cm wide and 175 cm long when measured unstretched. The alternating knit and purl columns stretch up to 25 cm wide when pulled gently. The scarf wraps close and holds its position around the neck without pinning.

Flat construction was chosen because a ribbed scarf worked flat in rows produces a rectangular fabric with no seam, no special cast-on technique, and no need to manage a circular needle join. The rib pattern is fully reversible, so there is no right or wrong side to track. The finished scarf uses about 150 g (340 m / 372 yards) of DK-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any DK yarn. A wool or wool-blend yarn gives the best stretch-and-recovery in rib.

content.text: Gauge

22 sts x 30 rows = 10 x 10 cm in 1x1 rib on 4.5 mm needles, measured unstretched and slightly relaxed after removing from the needles. Rib gauge must be measured after the swatch has rested off the needle for at least ten minutes; on the needle the swatch is compressed and reads narrower. Each stitch off gauge shifts the finished width by about 0.8 cm: at 20 sts per 10 cm the scarf finishes about 20 cm wide unstretched; at 24 sts it finishes about 17 cm.
Stitches used

K (knit), P (purl). In 1x1 rib, the yarn moves between the needles before each purl stitch (yarn to front) and after each purl stitch back to work (yarn to back). Moving the yarn between the wrong positions adds unwanted stitches; check the yarn position every time you change from knit to purl and from purl to knit.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 40 stitches on the needle. For an even rib, the cast-on should start and end with a knit stitch (an even number of stitches works for 1x1 rib). Tail length formula: tail_cm = (needle circumference in mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 4.5 mm needles and 40 stitches: (14.1 x 40) / 10 + 15 = about 71 cm.
Stitch count check-in: 40 stitches after the cast-on.
Body
Every row: (K1, P1) to end. (40 sts)

Work every row the same until the scarf measures 175 cm from the cast-on edge, measured along the straight grain with the piece lying flat and not stretched. This takes approximately 525 rows. At the halfway mark (about 87 cm), count the stitches: still 40.
Cast off
Use a
stretchy cast off

to match the elasticity of the rib body. Work the cast-off in pattern (K the knit stitches, P the purl stitches) and work loosely. A tight cast-off pulls in the top edge of the scarf and prevents it from sitting flat.
Common faults

Stitch count increases across the scarf. The most common cause is leaving the yarn in front at the start of a row when the first stitch is a knit: the yarn makes an unintended yarn-over and creates a new stitch. Always check the yarn is at the back before the first knit stitch of each row.

Rib columns that look broken or uneven. This happens when a knit stitch is worked as a purl or vice versa. The fix is to read the stitches as they sit on the needle: a V-shaped loop facing you is a knit stitch and should be knitted; a bump facing you is a purl stitch and should be purled.
Tight cast-off that pulls the top edge inward. Use a needle two sizes larger for the cast-off row, or work the stretchy cast-off described above.
Finishing

Weave in both yarn tails along the wrong-side of the rib columns. Ribbed pieces are not normally blocked flat: blocking removes the stretch. A gentle wash and lay flat to dry is enough. If the rib looks uneven, it will relax after the first wash.
Care

Handwash in cool water with wool wash, press out moisture gently, and lay flat to dry. Do not hang a wet ribbed piece: the weight of the water stretches the rib lengthways. For cotton or acrylic: follow the yarn label.
What to try next

The 2x2 ribbed scarf uses groups of two knit and two purl stitches to produce wider, more defined columns. Or try the seed-stitch scarf, where the knit and purl positions swap on every row to produce a textured, non-stretchy fabric.
